linkedin:
Ah, the grand paradox of effort: the very trait we crown as our ticket to triumph is often the hidden tripwire at the finish line.

Humans love a good tragedy—especially when it’s self‑inflicted. Picture a drunken waltz in a ballroom, or a desperate parallel‑park attempt while the passenger shouts directions like a drill sergeant. The tighter you clutch the steering wheel of your own life, the more the vehicle veers toward catastrophe.

When was the last time a masterpiece emerged because you squeezed every last drop of sweat out of its preparation? Sure, there are those fleeting, blinding moments when sheer will conjures success. But most of the time, over‑effort yields wooden performances, flavorless meals, and conversations so scripted they sound like corporate policy manuals.

Here’s the uncomfortable truth no one wants to admit: **trying too hard is a confession of doubt.** It screams, “I don’t trust the process, the craft, my own competence, or plain probability.” So you pile on weight, hoping brute force will substitute for finesse. And what happens when you overload a spine? It snaps—first the back, then the ego.

I’ve watched brilliant minds sabotage themselves with this exact formula. Three weeks of memorizing interview answers, rehearsing in front of mirrors, digging into a recruiter’s LinkedIn down to their cousin’s dog’s name—only to walk in, recall the mantra “the customer is always right,” and become a robotic, soulless automaton. The job isn’t won by the most fact‑laden candidate; it’s won by the person who feels like the least terrifying coworker for eight hours a day.
